summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring devices and clocks that use the Precision Time Protocol as specified in IEEE Std 1588-2008, and for retrieving configuration, data sets, and running state. It conforms to NMDA and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A settings and status sheet for devices that keep very exact time, written in a form that management software can read.

questions: what is the ptp yang model
how to configure ptp with netconf
subtitle: A YANG schema that lets management software configure and read Precision Time Protocol clocks.

tldr.problem: IEEE Std 1588-2008 clocks have many configuration parameters and state data sets, but the existing MIBs focus on reading state over SNMP and do not cover configuring PTP data sets.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-ptp YANG module, which models the IEEE 1588 data sets (default, current, parent, time properties, port, and transparent clock data sets) under a single ptp container, using YANG-style names.
tldr.outcome: Operators and controllers can configure PTP devices and retrieve their data sets and running state through YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF. The module follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

today: RFC 8575 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text expects the module to be revised when IEEE Std 1588 is revised, and describes a possible future transfer of IEEE 1588 YANG work to the IEEE.

sections.title: Why a YANG Model for PTP
sections.content:
IEEE Std 1588-2008 defines the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), which the RFC says can provide time synchronization as fine as nanoseconds and is widely supported in carrier, industrial and automotive networks. Its configuration parameters and state data sets are numerous.

The standard already has an information model for its data sets, and MIBs such as RFC 8173 cover them. The RFC points out that those MIBs focus on retrieving state data with SNMP, and that RFC 8173 does not consider configuring PTP data sets. Service providers want more flexible, Internet-based management, and Software-Defined Networking demands better configuration of synchronization networks.

YANG (RFC 7950) is a data modeling language for configuration and state data manipulated by protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241). The RFC lists its advantages as Internet-based configuration, validation and rollback. The model is based on the PTP data sets in IEEE 1588, and technology-specific information such as a bridge, router or telecom profile is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The old read-out panels could show what a clock was doing but could not change its settings. This one can do both.

sections.title: How the Module Is Meant to Be Used
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the reader already knows IEEE Std 1588-2008, and describes how the module fits into a larger family of models.

  • It can be used as is for products that conform to one of the default profiles specified in IEEE Std 1588-2008.
  • When IEEE 1588 is revised and adds optional features to its data sets, the module can be revised and extended. The YANG revision MUST be used to indicate such changes.
  • A profile standard may create its own YANG module. It SHOULD import this module and use augment for profile-specific additions.
  • A product that conforms to a profile may do the same with the profile's module, adding product-specific enhancements.

A profile is the way one industry, such as telecom or automotive, specifies how IEEE 1588 is used. A profile can require features that are optional in the base standard.
sections.eli5: The basic control panel is built so that other groups can bolt extra buttons onto it, instead of building a new panel from scratch.

sections.title: The Data Model Hierarchy
sections.content:
The module is rooted at a ptp container. Inside it, an instance-list holds one entry per PTP instance, keyed by instance-number. Each instance carries the clock data sets: default-ds, current-ds, parent-ds and time-properties-ds, plus a port-ds-list with one entry per port.

Outside the instance list, at the top of the ptp container, sit transparent-clock-default-ds and transparent-clock-port-ds-list. Attribute names follow IEEE 1588 but use YANG style: all lowercase, with dashes between words.

Examples of what the data sets hold include the clock quality (clock-class, clock-accuracy, offset-scaled-log-variance), priority1 and priority2, domain-number, offset and mean path delay, the parent and grandmaster identities, UTC offset and leap second flags, and per-port intervals such as log-announce-interval and log-sync-interval. The clock-identity of a clock is read-only.
sections.eli5: Think of a folder for each clock, with sheets inside for its identity, its current time error, its boss clock, and one sheet per plug-in port.

sections.title: Instances and Interpretations from the IEEE 1588 Working Group
sections.content:
The model differs subtly from the data set specifications of IEEE Std 1588-2008. The RFC says these differences come from the interpretation of the IEEE 1588 Working Group and aim at compatibility with future revisions.

A physical product can implement several PTP clocks, and each operates in an independent domain, but the data sets did not make clear how multiple domains are organized. The RFC therefore introduces the PTP instance: a PTP implementation in the device (an ordinary or boundary clock) represented by a specific PTP data set. Each instance operates in exactly one domain. The instance-number is used for management only and does not appear in PTP messages.

Most transparent clock products treat the transparent clock data sets as a singleton at the root of the managed product, based on IEEE 1588 subclauses 8.3.1 and 10.1, so the model puts them there.
sections.eli5: One box can pretend to be several clocks at once. Each pretend clock gets a label number so the manager knows which is which, but the number is never sent over the wire.

sections.title: Configuration and State
sections.content:
IEEE Std 1588-2008 classifies each data set member in one of three ways:

  • Configurable: writable by management.
  • Dynamic: read-only to management, with the value changed by PTP protocol operation.
  • Static: read-only, and the value typically does not change.

For details on any member, the RFC refers to the IEEE standard. If an implementation needs to change a classification, for example making a configurable member read-only, it SHOULD return a warning when the read-only member is written, or use the YANG deviation mechanism described in Section 7.20.3 of RFC 7950 to build a new deviation model.

The module itself imports the interface-ref type from RFC 8343 and defines types such as the delay mechanism (e2e, p2p, disabled) and the port state (initializing, faulty, disabled, listening, pre-master, master, passive, uncalibrated, slave).
sections.eli5: Some numbers on the panel are dials you can turn, and some are just gauges that move by themselves. The RFC says which is which.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

The sensitive writable subtrees are /ptp/instance-list, /ptp/transparent-clock-default-ds and /ptp/transparent-clock-port-ds-list. Writes without proper protection can harm network operations, for example through loss of synchronization on a clock, accuracy degradation on a set of clocks, or even the breakdown of a whole synchronization network. General security considerations for time protocols are in RFC 7384.
sections.eli5: Anyone who could twist the dials could make clocks disagree, so only trusted people should be allowed to touch them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and the Appendix on Transfer
sections.content:
The RFC registers the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ptp in the IETF XML Registry and the module name ietf-ptp, with prefix ptp, in the YANG Module Names registry.

An informational appendix describes a future plan to transfer responsibility for IEEE 1588 YANG modules from the IETF TICTOC Working Group to the IEEE 1588 Working Group. It states that it is forward-looking and specifies nothing normative. It covers assumptions for the transfer, intellectual property (the authors assigned a non-exclusive license so IEEE can create derivative works), and the namespace and module name.
sections.eli5: The module gets an official name in the registry, and the authors note that the IEEE group that owns the clock standard may take over the module one day.
